children.blurb: Personalised learning and early warning covers systems that adapt content, pace, or feedback to individual learners and that flag students at risk of falling behind or dropping out.

children.name: Course-Specific AI Tutors
children.blurb: Course-specific AI tutors are software systems configured for a single course or module, drawing on that course's syllabus, readings, problem sets, and assessment criteria to answer student questions and give feedback.

children.blurb: Lecture materials from notes covers the conversion of an instructor's raw notes, marginal annotations, and outline fragments into structured teaching artifacts such as slide decks, handouts, discussion prompts, and study guides.

sections.body: This field covers how artificial intelligence is used to plan courses, write tests, adjust teaching to individual students, run subject specific tutors, and turn notes into lecture materials. In practice, systems now map course content to learning outcomes by comparing syllabus text against outcome statements. They generate quiz questions and exam drafts from source material, flag students who may be falling behind using activity data, answer student questions inside a single course, and convert a lecturer's notes into slide decks or study guides. These are working tools, not just proposals, and they are being tried in real classrooms and online courses.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Generating a first draft of a multiple choice quiz is fairly reliable, but open ended marking and feedback still need human review. Personalised learning systems can spot patterns in clicks and grades, yet they often cannot explain why a student is struggling or what to change next. Course specific tutors work best when the subject has clear right and wrong answers, like introductory programming or mathematics, and much less well in discussion based or creative fields. The honest limit is that these tools assist a teacher, they do not replace one, and their output can be confidently wrong.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader looking for how courses are planned should start with Curriculum and Learning Outcomes, which shows how AI compares teaching content to stated goals. Generating Assessments covers the creation of tests and marking rubrics, including what can be automated and what cannot. Personalised Learning and Early Warning explains the data driven side, where systems try to adjust pace or raise alerts. Course-Specific AI Tutors is the place for subject focused question answering and practice, while Lecture Materials from Notes shows the conversion of raw notes into usable teaching resources. Together they move from planning, to testing, to adapting, to direct student support, and finally to preparing the materials that tie the course together.
